questions.q: Why don't Python threads help speed up CPU-bound work in CPython?
options: Threads are only available on Linux
The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, even on a multi-core machine
Threads automatically run slower than a single-process loop
Python threads cannot call functions that use NumPy
questions.explain: CPython's GIL means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time; for CPU-bound work this means threads effectively take turns on one core rather than running in parallel, unlike I/O-bound work where the GIL is released while waiting.

questions.q: Why does code using `ProcessPoolExecutor` need an `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard?
options: It's purely a style convention with no functional effect
Spawning a worker process re-imports the module; without the guard, that re-import would try to spawn the pool again, recursively
It is required only when using joblib, not ProcessPoolExecutor
It prevents the GIL from being created
questions.explain: Especially on Windows (which uses the spawn method), a new process re-imports the launching module -- without the __main__ guard, that re-import re-executes the pool-creation code, recursively spawning more processes.

questions.q: What is the main cost that `joblib.Parallel`/`delayed` and `ProcessPoolExecutor` both incur when sending work to a worker process?
options: Compiling the function to machine code
Pickling (serializing) arguments and return values to send them across process boundaries
Converting the function to Cython
Re-running the GIL initialization
questions.explain: Every argument and return value crossing a process boundary must be pickled by the sender and unpickled by the receiver, which has real overhead, especially for large objects.

questions.q: In the measured 'tiny task' example (x + 1 run 200 times), what happened when it was parallelized across processes?
options: It ran about 4x faster, matching the number of CPU cores
It ran over 12,000x slower than the serial version, because process/pickling overhead vastly exceeded the trivial computation
It produced incorrect results
It ran at exactly the same speed as serial
questions.explain: The measured numbers showed serial at 0.025 ms vs. parallel at 320.703 ms -- a clear case where the per-task overhead of multiprocessing dwarfed the actual (trivial) work being done.

questions.q: Based on this lesson, what rule of thumb determines whether a task is worth parallelizing across processes?
options: Any task, no matter how small, benefits from parallelization
Only tasks that use NumPy benefit
Each task should be expensive enough (roughly tens of milliseconds or more) that the fixed per-task process/pickling overhead doesn't dominate the actual work
Parallelization only works for tasks that take exactly 1 second
questions.explain: Multiprocessing has real, fixed overhead per task from process coordination and pickling; it only pays off once each unit of work is substantial enough that this overhead is a small fraction of the total.
